lesson.title: Under the Root: Simplifying and Taming Radical Expressions
lesson.summary: A radical expression is really a fractional exponent in different clothing, and simplifying, combining, and rationalizing radicals all lean on the exponent and factoring skills from the last two chapters.
lesson.body:
A square root sign is just another way to write a fractional exponent: the square root of x is the same thing as x raised to the 1/2 power, and the cube root of x is x raised to the 1/3 power. Keeping that connection in mind explains why radicals follow rules that look so similar to exponent rules, they are exponent rules, applied to fractional powers.

To simplify a radical like the square root of a number that is not a perfect square, look for the largest perfect square factor hiding inside it, the same factoring instinct from the previous chapter. The square root of a product splits into the product of the square roots, so the square root of (a times b) equals the square root of a times the square root of b. If a is a perfect square, that piece simplifies to a whole number and comes out from under the radical.

Radicals combine the same way like terms do in a polynomial: you can only add or subtract radicals that have the same expression underneath the root, called the radicand. Three square roots of two plus five square roots of two combine to eight square roots of two, exactly the way 3x + 5x combines to 8x, because in both cases you are counting how many copies of the same unit you have.

A fraction with a radical left in the denominator is usually considered unsimplified on the ACT, so the last step is rationalizing the denominator, multiplying the top and bottom of the fraction by whatever radical is needed to turn the denominator into a whole number. Multiplying the square root of a number by itself removes the radical entirely, since the square root of a times the square root of a equals a.

Simplify the square root of 72 first. Since 72 equals 36 times 2, and 36 is a perfect square, the square root of 72 equals the square root of 36 times the square root of 2, which is 6 times the square root of 2, usually written 6 root 2. Check this by squaring the answer: (6 root 2)^2 equals 36 times 2, which is 72, matching the original number under the root.

Now rationalize 5 divided by the square root of 3. Multiply top and bottom by the square root of 3: (5 times the square root of 3) divided by (the square root of 3 times the square root of 3), which is (5 root 3) divided by 3, since the square root of 3 times itself equals 3. Check this numerically: the square root of 3 is approximately 1.732, so 5 divided by 1.732 is approximately 2.887, and 5 times 1.732 divided by 3 is 8.660 divided by 3, also approximately 2.887. The two values match.

These same radical skills return in the very next chapter, since the quadratic formula produces a square root that often needs to be simplified exactly the way the square root of 72 was simplified here.
